RE: Project No. 58481, Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards under PURA 37.0561;
Project No. 59142, Review of ERCOT’s Interconnection Processes for Large Loads

4/9/2026


Vistra is filing a courtesy copy of its comments submitted today on Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 145
in the above-referenced Commission control numbers. As with Vistra’s March 20, 2026-filed PGRR145 comments
PGRR145, these comments also address interactions between the Proposal for Publication (PFP) in Project No.
58481, the recently-adopted 16 TAC § 25.205, and the proposed Batch Zero timeline and transition criteria. Vistra
intends to include consistent commentary in its formal rulemaking comments in Project No. 58481, and offers these
for the Commission’s consideration in anticipation of discussion at the April 17, 2026 open meeting.

Vistra continues to believe that these provisions, in combination, risk confounding the statutory deadlines for review
of Net Metering Arrangements subject to PURA § 39.169 (the “39.169 NMAs”). To mitigate the risk of inequitable
impacts and support compliance with the deadlines in PURA § 39.169(d) while also respecting the new provisions
of 16 TAC § 25.205 and ERCOT’s preference to have all incremental 2028+ energizations evaluated under the
Batch process, Vistra offers a simplified approach, relative to its prior comments, to minimizing (and ideally avoiding)
timing inconsistencies between PGRR145 and PURA § 39.169(d):
    • 39.169 NMAs with an assigned Large Load Interconnection Number (LLI#) and initial energization date on
         or before December 31, 2027, as well as any 39.169 NMAs with applications approved or pending at the
         Commission as of July 10, 2026, will be studied under the Legacy Large Load Interconnection process and
         included in Batch Zero base load.
    • Other 39.169 NMAs with an assigned LLI# and initial energization date between January 1, 2028 and
         December 31, 2028 (and not already included in base load) will be included in Batch Zero as load to be
         studied and allocated in Batch Zero.
    • PGRR145 language should also specify that the System Protection (Short Circuit) Analysis is not required
         to be completed prior to the initiation of a 39.169 NMA notice to ERCOT and application to the Commission.
         This is not an exemption, simply stating that the 39.169 NMA process can begin prior to its completion.

This approach should help to ensure that 39.169 NMAs can proceed with minimal impact to the statutory timelines
in PURA § 39.169 and improve regulatory certainty, especially for those with nearer-term energization dates and
those that have already begun their statutory review prior to the changes proposed in PGRR145 taking effect.

Vistra’s latest PGRR145 comments continue to seek sufficient flexibility to include the full range of large load
configurations, and many of these comments are also relevant to the PFP in Project No. 58481. Vistra has offered
in these new comments alternative streamlined language to the same effect of the language offered in Vistra’s prior
PGRR145 comments, but either approach will help to appropriately assign party status to intermediate and
 interconnection agreements for Large Loads that will not take retail electric delivery service from a DSP. As stated
previously, this change should not impact the majority of Large Load intermediate and interconnection agreements
as proposed in Project No. 58481 (and in PGRR145), but helps to ensure all scenarios can work within the proposed
new procedures.

Additionally with respect to Project No. 58481 specifically, Vistra expresses conceptual support in these comments
for raising the $/MW financial security amount for Large Loads greater than 250 MW at the intermediate agreement
stage, particularly if paired with greater refundability. Vistra believes this could help to demonstrate access to capital
necessary to execute on an approved interconnection, which should help to ensure that viable long-term Large
Loads are energized timely and commensurate with the new transmission infrastructure necessary to serve them,
in turn helping to mitigate risk of burdening other customer classes with that transmission cost.

Other comments that are equally applicable to the Project No. 58481 PFP as well as its incorporation into PGRR145,
Vistra offers the following:
    • The site control provisions should be modified to specify that the Large Load is providing “evidence of
         sufficient” property interests to the Interconnecting TSP or DSP, as applicable. The Large Load will not be
         granting a property interest, however. Furthermore, the site control demonstration criteria should all be able
         to demonstrate the same durable interest (i.e., at least five years from the date the Large Load is expected
         to reach its contracted peak demand).
    • The requirement for ERCOT to reallocate withdrawn Requested or Contracted Peak Demand should
         specify that the reallocation will occur “in a future Batch Study” (or “interconnection study” may be more
         appropriate for the rule). This is critical to avoid a Batch Study and/or Batch Refinement Study falling into
         similar but different “do-loops” that could hinder forward progress.
    • The Large Load should be disclosing whether it “will be registered and operated” as a Controllable Load
         Resource (CLR), not whether it “can be modeled” as a CLR.
    • Vistra recognizes concerns raised about the timeline for refund of financial security post-energization in
         proposed Section 9.7.4 being potentially too short to offset the risk of cost-shifting to other customer classes
         if the refund is completed at only 5 years post-energization. Vistra has not proposed specific redlines, but
         agrees that other customer classes should not bear the risk of infrastructure costs outliving the large loads
         they were meant to serve.
    • Vistra continues to flag that there are several provisions ported over from the Commission’s Project No.
         58481 PFP that exceed the reasonable authority of the ERCOT Planning Guide. Vistra has not proposed
         any redlines at this time to PGRR145, but supports “right-sizing” PGRR145 accordingly.

There are additional issues addressed in these PGRR145 comments, though more specific to PGRR145 and not
as closely related to the Commission’s pending or recently-adopted rules. These are summarized in the narrative
of the PGRR145 comments. The only item that Vistra will call out here is that Vistra recommends that Large Loads
seeking approval in the May 1, 2027 Quarterly Stability Assessment (QSA) deadline not be forced into Batch Zero,
as that is the QSA that will evaluate 4Q2027 energizations (vs. Batch Zero that will only apply to 2028+ loads).


Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me at (512) 349-6464.


Best Regards,




Ned Bonskowski

  Vistra Operations Company LLC (Vistra) appreciates the opportunity to provide additional
  comments, this time in response to ERCOT’s April 4, 2026 comments on Planning Guide
  Revision Request (PGRR) 145. Vistra offers these comments to clarify and reply to
  ERCOT’s high-level summaries of Vistra’s March 20, 2026 comments, as well as to
  provide preliminary comments regarding the Public Utility Commission of Texas’
  (Commission) Proposal for Publication (PFP) in Project No. 58481.
  Vistra continues to have concerns regarding (1) incongruities with the Senate Bill 6 (SB6)
  statutory timeline for evaluating system impacts of Large Loads co-located with existing
  generators; (2) adding flexibility to the new references to Interconnecting DSPs and
  Interconnecting TSPs to account for the full diversity of Large Load configurations; and
  (3) comments on Project No. 58481 incorporations in PGRR145. Most of these concerns
  are reiterated in these comments. Vistra also includes a handful of relatively minor
  suggestions outside of these themes.


  Reconciling the Senate Bill 6 Timeline Incompatibility with Batch Zero
  As a threshold matter, Vistra supports the Batch study approach as clearly appropriate
  for the ~89% of the Large Load Interconnection Queue that is directly interconnected to
  the transmission system and not co-located with a generation resource, as well as for the
  portion of the remaining ~11% that are co-located with new generation resources not
  subject to PURA § 39.169. And, as Vistra noted in its March 20, 2026 comments, there
  are likely also times that the Batch study approach may also be the preference for some
  Large Loads entering into net metering arrangements with existing generators subject to
  PURA § 39.169 (the “39.169 NMAs”). Vistra remains concerned that the Batch process
  and associated timeline can also be inconsistent with the plain language of PURA §
  39.169(d), which was penned in the context and presumption of the TSP-driven Large
  Load Interconnection Study (LLIS) process that underpinned the 2022-2025 interim Large

Load interconnection process as well as PGRR115, which was being finalized
simultaneously with SB6.
However, recognizing that the scope of PGRR145 only extends to Batch Zero and the
transition of in-flight projects between the PGRR115 (soon-to-become “Legacy”) process
and Batch Zero, Vistra offers a simplified approach to minimizing (and ideally avoiding)
timing inconsistencies between PGRR145 and PURA § 39.169(d):
        39.169 NMAs with an assigned Large Load Interconnection Number (LLI#) and
         initial energization date on or before December 31, 2027, as well as any 39.169
         NMAs with applications approved or pending at the Commission as of July 10,
         2026, will be studied under the Legacy Large Load Interconnection process
         retained in PG145’s Sections 9.9-9.10, and included in base load under
         PGRR145’s Section 9.2.1.1.
        39.169 NMAs with an assigned LLI# and initial energization date between January
         1, 2028 and December 31, 2028 and not already included in base load will be
         included in Batch Zero as load to be studied and allocated in Batch Zero under
         PGRR 145’s Section 9.2.1.2.
The provisions in the first bullet ensure that a 39.169 NMA with an initial energization date
prior to Batch Zero’s energization window starting in 2028, or that has a pending or
recently-approved 39.169 NMA application before the Commission is not unnecessarily
delayed in its energization. This is pragmatic and respects both the statutory deadlines in
PURA § 39.169 and the recently-adopted rule requirements of the Commission’s 16 TAC
§ 25.205(d)(1)(B) because both the interconnection study and the Commission’s NMA
proceeding would need to be complete for such projects prior to January 1, 2028 (when
the first Batch Zero energization window opens).
The provisions in the second bullet help to minimize any delays to 39.169 NMAs with a
2028 initial energization date by assessing those that are not already included in base
load but have an assigned LLI# in Batch Zero. While not perfect because there are likely
some potential 39.169 NMAs that would still face procedural delays from this approach, 1
there are likely also counter examples of 39.169 NMAs that would face little or no delay
from this approach (even if procedurally very compact). Thus, this proposal is also
pragmatic as it should broadly allow reconciliation of ERCOT’s preference to have all
incremental 2028+ energizations evaluated under the Batch process with the PURA §
39.169(d) deadlines as implemented by 16 TAC § 25.205. Given the uncertainty of how
these issues may be in conflict for Batch 1+, Vistra recommends that the in-service date
window for this provision to extend through the end of 2028 (as a buffer against any delay
in Batch 1+ adoption/initiation).
Furthermore, Vistra recommends that PGRR145 explicitly state that the System
Protection (Short-Circuit) Analysis is not required to be completed prior to the initiation of
a net metering arrangement notice and application under PURA § 39.169. Because

PGRR145’s Section 9.3.1(3) sets a May 2, 2027 deadline2 for the interconnecting utility
to complete the System Protection (Short-Circuit) Analysis, this is a material contributor
to Vistra’s concern with the interplay between PGRR145’s Batch Zero timeline and the
PURA § 39.169 timeline. The recently-adopted 16 TAC § 25.205(d) & (g) require a
“completed large load interconnection study as the term is defined in the ERCOT
protocols [or another study required by ERCOT protocols] as of the date the application
is filed with the commission” as a prerequisite to filing the net metering arrangement
approval application. Therefore, requiring the System Protection (Short-Circuit) Analysis
to be complete as part of that package adds to the timing risk between Batch Zero and
PURA § 39.169(d). But by specifying in the Planning Guide that the System Protection
(Short-Circuit) Analysis need not be complete to initiate the net metering arrangement
approval process, the requirements of 16 TAC § 25.205(d) & (g) are still respected and
the System Protection (Short-Circuit) Analysis is still completed prior to energization – it
simply is removed as a potential added timeline drag on 39.169 NMAs under PGRR145
as proposed. Vistra offers this clarification in both proposed Section 9.3.1(3) and in
Section 9.5.2.


Flexibility to Include Full Diversity of Large Load Configurations
Vistra appreciates ERCOT’s comments on this recommendation expressing willingness
to consider this change. Vistra reiterates its prior comments and recommends that
ERCOT include Vistra’s recommended language (or substantively similar language) in
PGRR145 rather than re-evaluating in a future revision request. While Vistra supports the
revisions in its March 20, 2026 comments proposed to Sections 9.7.1(1) and 9.7.2(1), in
these comments Vistra offers potentially more streamlined language that simplifies the
determination of whether the Interconnecting Large Load Entity (ILLE) must contract with
both the Interconnecting Transmission Service Provider (TSP) and the Interconnecting
Distribution Service Provider (DSP) or only the Interconnecting TSP based on whether or
not the ILLE will take retail electric delivery service from a DSP. Vistra also suggests that
disclosure of this status would be appropriate to integrate into the power procurement
plans disclosure under proposed Section 9.7.1(g).


Comments on Project No. 58481 PFP Incorporations in PGRR145
Vistra supports robust financial commitment criteria that can help demonstrate that an
ILLE has the access to capital and other means necessary to execute on approved
interconnection requests. This will help to ensure that the Large Load is able to execute
and in turn pay its fair share of transmission costs, efficiently utilizing existing
infrastructure and avoiding those costs being allocated to residential and small
commercial customers.
While Vistra has not proposed specific redlines in these comments, Vistra would support
a two-tiered $/MW financial security requirement for the Intermediate Agreement in
Section 9.7.1(1)(i), particularly if paired with greater refundability. While the Commission
modified the Project No. 58481 Proposal for Publication (PFP) to reduce the financial

security from $100,000/MW to $50,000/MW amid concerns that doing so might
overburden some large load projects, particularly non-data center large loads, Vistra
notes that the costs to develop a data center can be in the hundreds of millions of dollars
to more than $1 billion before even introducing server and chip costs. Vistra also suspects
that the vast majority of large loads > 250 MW are data center projects and for such
projects being able to demonstrate access to capital will help to ensure that the most
viable projects move forward first, which is critical during a time when stakeholders and
policymakers alike want to ensure that viable long-term loads are energized timely and
commensurate with the new transmission infrastructure necessary to serve them in order
to avoid burdening other customer classes with that transmission buildout. Therefore,
applying a higher $/MW financial security value for large loads > 250 MW may be a
reasonable test for access to capital needed to actually take on the much larger cost of
building the consuming facility (after all, even at $100,000/MW, a 250 MW data center
would only need to post $25 million – a material sum in the abstract, but a relatively very
small percentage of the project construction costs). Vistra is open to other MW-based
tiering points, but notes that there is precedent for bifurcating costs at a 250 MW level in
the Project No. 58481 PFP, which triples the study fee for large loads ≥ 250 MW vs. those
that are in the 75 MW to 250 MW range. To balance against the risks of under-allocation
that many stakeholders have raised, given the need to post financial security prior to the
Batch study, if a tiered higher financial security provision is considered, it would be
appropriate to pair that with a higher refundability provision than the currently proposed
maximum 20%.
As for specific comments on Project No. 58481 PFP incorporations into PGRR145, Vistra
offers the following:
      The site control provisions in Sections 9.7.1(1)(a) and 9.7.2(1)(a) should both be
       modified to specify that the ILLE is providing “evidence of sufficient” property
       interests to the Interconnecting TSP or DSP. The ILLE will not be granting a
       property interest, however. Furthermore, the site control demonstration criteria
       should all be able to demonstrate the same durable interest (i.e., at least five years
       from the date the ILLE is expected to reach its contracted peak demand).
      The requirement for ERCOT to reallocate withdrawn Requested or Contracted
       Peak Demand in proposed Section 9.7.3(1)(f) should specify that the reallocation
       will occur “in a future Batch Study.” This is critical to avoid a Batch Study and/or
       Batch Refinement Study falling into similar but different “do-loops” that could hinder
       forward progress.
      In Section 9.7.1(1)(h), the ILLE should be disclosing whether it “will be registered
       and operated” as a CLR, not whether it “can be modeled” as a CLR.
      Vistra recognizes concerns raised about the timeline for refund of financial security
       post-energization in proposed Section 9.7.4 being potentially too short to offset the
       risk of cost-shifting to other customer classes if the refund is completed at only 5
       years post-energization. Vistra has not proposed specific redlines, but agrees that
       other customer classes should not bear the risk of infrastructure costs outliving the
       large loads they were meant to serve.

      Vistra continues to flag that there are several provisions ported over from the
       Commission’s Project No. 58481 PFP that exceed the reasonable authority of the
       ERCOT Planning Guide. Vistra has not proposed any redlines at this time to
       PGRR145, but supports “right-sizing” PGRR145 accordingly.


Other Minor Recommendations
Vistra includes a few comparatively minor redlines in these comments:
      Vistra continues to recommend that Large Loads seeking approval in the May 1,
       2027 QSA deadline not be forced into Batch Zero, as that is the QSA that will
       evaluate 4Q2027 energizations (vs. Batch Zero that will only apply to 2028+ loads).
      Establish a date certain for the applicable DWG Procedure Manual that applies to
       the July 10, 2026 demonstration deadline. Vistra recommends anchoring to the
       current DWG Procedure Manual as of March 4, 2026 in Section 9.2.2(3).
      Specify in Section 9.2.3(2) that an ILLE must “promptly” provide updated dynamic
       data reflecting changes to load composition, technology, or parameters upon
       notification that a change in one of those parameters has occurred.
      ERCOT may wish to have flexibility under Section 9.5.1(5) to submit its final Batch
       Zero report to RPG as a single project or divided into regional sub-reports.
      Update the cross-reference in Section 9.5.2(2) to reference ERCOT base cases
       posted per Section 9.3.2(3) instead of 9.3.2(2), since ERCOT’s April 4, 2026
       comments added a new 9.3.2(2).
      Specify the Protected Information references in Sections 9.7.1(1)(b)(iv) and
       9.7.2(1)(b)(iv).
      Include the missing term “Legacy” in the title reference to Section 9.8.2 in Section
       9.8.1(3) and to Section 9.8.4 in Section 9.9(2).

comments received on March 20 in the matrix in ERCOT’s April 4, 2026 comments. Vistra

3.1.3.1         Definitions of Reliability-Driven and Economic-Driven Projects

(1)       Proposed transmission projects are categorized for evaluation purposes into two types:

          (a)      Reliability-driven projects; and

          (b)      Economic-driven projects.

(2)       The differentiation between these two types of projects is based on whether a
          simultaneously-feasible, security-constrained generating unit commitment and dispatch is
          expected to be available for all hours of the planning horizon that can resolve the system
          reliability issue that the proposed project is intended to resolve. If it is not possible to
          simulate a dispatch of the Generation Resources and ESRs such that all reliability criteria
          are met without the project, and the addition of the project allows the reliability criteria to
          be met, then the project is classified as a reliability-driven project. If it is possible to
          simulate a dispatch of the Generation Resources and ESRs in such a way that all
          reliability criteria are met without the project, but the project may allow the reliability
          criteria to be met at a lower total cost, then the project is classified as an economic-driven
          project. When performing a simulation of the generating unit commitment and dispatch,
          only contingencies and limits that would be considered in the operations horizon shall be
          simulated.

        agreed by the TSP(s) in the interconnection study agreement.

        simulations of the existing and proposed ERCOT transmission system. The results from

9.8.3        Legacy Large Load Interconnection Study Description and Methodology

(1)       The primary purpose of the LLIS is to determine whether the amount of Load being
          requested by the ILLE can be placed in service by the desired Initial Energization date
          while maintaining the reliability of the ERCOT System and ensuring compliance with all
          North American Reliability Corporation (NERC) Reliability Standards, Protocols, this
          Planning Guide, and the Operating Guides. The LLIS will also identify any transmission
          improvements needed to serve the full requested Load amount, including individual load
          increments requested by the ILLE in the initial Load Commissioning Plan (LCP).

(2)       The LLIS consists of a series of distinct study elements. The specific elements included
          in a particular LLIS will be stated in the LLIS scope.

(3)       Each proposed Large Load interconnection that requests more than one physical
          transmission interconnection will be studied as an individual study for each
          interconnection to be analyzed separately from all other such requests unless otherwise
          agreed by the TSP(s) in the interconnection study agreement.

(4)       The LLIS process includes developing and analyzing various computer model
          simulations of the existing and proposed ERCOT transmission system. The results from
          these simulations will be utilized by the TSP(s) to determine the impact of the proposed
          interconnection.

(5)       The study shall include an analysis demonstrating the adequate reliability of any
          temporary interconnection configurations.
